turns.message:
You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual ARC

1. On every turn, end with exactly one permitted action JSON object: `submit` with a valid grid, `request_demos`, or `finish` only after the instance is over. Keep explanation out of evaluator-facing replies.
2. Establish the structural parse before guessing a transformation: record input/output dimensions for every demo, identify repeated divider rows/columns and their intervals, then locate which cells encode the output. Use the actual demo outputs to determine how many regions or markers are emitted; never infer output dimensions from the test lattice alone. Track exact colors and positions and test the proposed rule against every demo before applying it to the test.
3. Request a demo only when you can name the competing hypotheses it will separate and the information is worth its cost. After an incorrect submission, revise the transformation itself using that counterevidence; do not repeat a guessed output or change only an unsupported detail. Submit only after checking the proposed output's dimensions and entries against the verified rule. If unresolved uncertainty remains, prefer a discriminating demo over a fabricated grid when its expected value justifies the cost.
